items.claim: The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission has the authority to apply the collateral source rule when awarding past pecuniary damages against a federal agency under 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-16(b), allowing it to decline to deduct insurance benefits received by a claimant through the Federal Employees Health Benefits program.

items.case_holding_text: When the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission awards past pecuniary damages against a federal agency pursuant to 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-16(b), it may apply the collateral source rule to decline to deduct insurance benefits that a claimant received through the Federal Employees Health Benefits program.

items.claim: The Court of Claims dismissed the breach of contract claim based on a collective bargaining agreement for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction.
items.case_holding_text: The Court of Claims did not err in granting Ohio State University's ("OSU") motion for summary judgment on the employment discrimination claim or in dismissing the breach of contract claim based on a collective bargaining agreement for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction.

items.case_name: Norman v. N.C. Dep't of Admin.
items.case_holding_text:
we hold that summary judgment was proper.

      A. Standard of Review

      Summary judgment is appropriate when the “the pleadings, depositions,

answers to interrogatories, and admissions on file, together with the affidavits, if any,

show that there is no genuine issue as to any material fact and that any party is

entitled to a judgment as a matter of law.” N.C. Gen. Stat. § 1A-1, Rule 56(c) (2015).



                                          -6-
                                    NORMAN V. NCDOA

                                   Opinion of the Court



The party moving for summary judgment bears the initial burden of proof, which may

be met “(1) by showing an essential element of the opposing party’s claim is

nonexistent or cannot be proven, or (2) by showing through discovery that the

opposing party cannot produce evidence to support an essential element of his or her

claim.” Belcher v. Fleetwood Enters., Inc., 162 N.C. App. 80, 84, 590 S.E.2d 15, 18

(2004).

      Upon a forecast of evidence tending to support the motion for summary

judgment, the burden shifts to the non-moving party to likewise “produce a forecast

of evidence demonstrating that [she] will be able to make out at least a prima facie

case at trial.” Collingwood v. Gen. Electric Real Estate Equities, Inc., 324 N.C. 63, 66,

276 S.E.2d 425, 427 (1989) (citation omitted). The non-moving party survives the

motion not by “rest[ing] upon the mere allegations” of her pleading, N.C. Gen. Stat. §

1A-1, Rule 56(e) (2015); rather, she “must come forward with specific facts showing a

genuine issue for trial.” Beaver v. Hancock, 72 N.C. App. 306, 310, 324 S.E.2d 294,

298 (1985) (citation omitted). In evaluating a motion for summary judgment, the trial

court must view the evidence in the light most favorable to the non-moving party,

and all inferences of fact must be drawn in her favor. In re Estate of Redding v.

Welborn, 170 N.C. App. 324, 329, 612 S.E.2d 664, 668 (2005). “Our standard of review

of an appeal from summary judgment is de novo[.]” In re Will of Jones, 362 N.C. 569,

573, 669 S.E.2d 572, 576 (2008).

items.claim: Plaintiff was assigned to work at a business by a contractor.
items.case_holding_text: Grant of summary judgment was proper in employment discrimination case where plaintiff failed to show existence of employment relationship between herself and business where she was assigned to work by contractor.
items.source_text_used: Grant of summary judgment was proper in employment discrimination case where plaintiff failed to show existence of employment relationship between herself and business where she was assigned to work by contractor.

items.claim: Hughes failed to demonstrate a prima facie case of discrimination in his employment discrimination claim against YSU.
items.case_holding_text: The trial court did not err in granting YSU's motion for summary judgment on Hughes' claim of employment discrimination as Hughes failed to demonstrate a prima facie case of discrimination.
items.source_text_used: The trial court did not err in granting YSU's motion for summary judgment on Hughes' claim of employment discrimination as Hughes failed to demonstrate a prima facie case of discrimination.

items.claim: An employer's repeated assignment of a minority employee to less desirable shifts, despite equivalent seniority and performance reviews, constitutes an adverse employment action sufficient to sustain a Title VII disparate treatment claim. The court held that discriminatory scheduling patterns need not culminate in termination to be actionable under federal employment discrimination law.
items.citation: Delgado v. Hartwell Manufacturing Corp., 883 F.3d 214 (2nd Cir. 2020)

items.claim: An employer's reliance on subjective supervisory evaluations as the sole basis for promotion decisions constitutes circumstantial evidence of discriminatory intent under Title VII when the workforce demographics reveal a statistically significant racial disparity in advancement rates.
items.citation: Bellard v. Transcontinental Industries, Inc., 634 F.2d 271 (D.C. Cir. 1981)

items.claim: An employer's repeated failure to promote a qualified minority employee while advancing less experienced white colleagues with similar job functions constitutes sufficient circumstantial evidence of discriminatory intent to survive summary judgment under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
items.citation: Whitfield v. Meridian Industrial Services, Inc., 284 F.3d 512 (4th Cir. 1997)
items.case_name: Whitfield v. Meridian Industrial Services, Inc.

items.claim: An employer's reliance on subjective criteria in promotion decisions, when applied disproportionately against a protected class, may constitute sufficient evidence of discriminatory intent under Title VII. The court held that statistical disparities combined with documented supervisor bias can establish a prima facie case of employment discrimination.
items.citation: Dellworth v. Coastal Shipping & Transport Co., 778 F.2d 341 (11th Cir. 1986)
items.case_name: Dellworth v. Coastal Shipping & Transport Co.

items.claim: An employer's repeated exclusion of a qualified candidate from promotion consideration, coupled with documented remarks referencing the candidate's national origin, is sufficient to establish a prima facie case of discriminatory intent under Title VII. The court held that statistical disparities in promotion rates alone, when corroborated by direct supervisory statements, may defeat a motion for summary judgment.
items.citation: Weston v. Meridian Financial Group, Inc., 731 F.3d 214 (2nd Cir. 2014)
items.case_name: Weston v. Meridian Financial Group, Inc.
